clinicalPearls: A dose-dependent illness following whole-body or large partial-body exposure to high-dose ionising radiation
The clinical course classically passes through prodromal, latent and manifest illness phases
The dominant subsyndrome depends on dose: haematopoietic at lower, gastrointestinal at higher and neurovascular at the highest exposures
Early and severe nausea and vomiting and a rapid fall in lymphocyte count indicate a higher dose and worse prognosis
The rate of decline of the absolute lymphocyte count over the first days is a useful biological dosimeter
Management is supportive, including infection prevention, blood product support and growth factors, with specific measures for internal contamination
reference.pathophysiology: Acute radiation syndrome results from radiation-induced damage to rapidly dividing cells, especially in the bone marrow, gastrointestinal mucosa and, at extreme doses, the vascular and nervous systems. Ionising radiation causes DNA damage and cell death in proliferating tissues, so the marrow fails with resulting cytopenias and infection risk, and at higher doses the gut mucosal barrier breaks down causing fluid loss, bleeding and sepsis. The highest exposures cause cardiovascular collapse and neurological injury. The timing and severity of each subsyndrome scale with the absorbed dose.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis or other cause of pancytopenia
Acute gastroenteritis or other cause of vomiting and diarrhoea
Other toxic or chemical mass-exposure illness
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood counts with attention to lymphocyte depletion kinetics
Estimation of absorbed dose from exposure history and biological dosimetry
Assessment for external contamination and internal radionuclide uptake
Monitoring for infection, bleeding and fluid and electrolyte disturbance
redFlags: Early-onset, severe vomiting soon after exposure
Neurological or cardiovascular collapse indicating a very high dose
Signs of gastrointestinal barrier failure and sepsis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is strongly dose-dependent: haematopoietic-range exposures are often survivable with intensive support, whereas gastrointestinal and neurovascular syndromes carry high to near-certain mortality.
pitfalls: Underestimating dose when early symptoms seem mild during the latent phase
Neglecting lymphocyte-count kinetics as a dosimeter
Overlooking internal contamination requiring specific decorporation
Failing to protect staff and manage contamination during care
